interactions.label: A 45-year-old man dies 18 hours after admission to casualty with no confirmed di

params.question: A 45-year-old man dies 18 hours after admission to casualty with no confirmed diagnosis. The attending emergency physician is asked to issue the MCCD. What should the physician do?

answers.text: Issue the MCCD listing 'cause unknown' as the underlying cause

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An MCCD cannot be issued with an unknown cause. When death occurs within 24 hours of admission without a confirmed diagnosis, the case must be referred for medicolegal investigation.

answers.text: Refer the body for medicolegal investigation, as death occurred within 24 hours without a known cause

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Under the RBD Act framework, death within 24 hours of admission with no confirmed cause is one of the specific situations where the attending physician cannot issue the MCCD — the body must be referred for inquest and possible forensic autopsy.

answers.text: Request the most senior physician in the hospital to sign the certificate instead

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Seniority alone does not confer authority to certify. The certifying doctor must have personal knowledge of the case — either through treating the patient during the final illness or examining the body afterward.

answers.text: Issue the MCCD based on the clinical presentation at the time of admission

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Issuing a certificate based on an unconfirmed presentation when the actual cause of death is unknown would be inaccurate and potentially fraudulent, exposing the doctor to legal liability.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the situations where the attending physician is not permitted to issue the MCCD. Death within 24 hours of admission with no known cause requires referral for medicolegal investigation.
Well done. Deaths within 24 hours without a confirmed diagnosis must be referred for medicolegal investigation — the attending physician cannot certify these directly.

interactions.label: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) develops pneumonia,

params.question: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) develops pneumonia, which leads to respiratory failure and death. When applying ICD-11, which condition should be assigned the code?

answers.text: Respiratory failure, because it is the immediate mechanism of death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Coding the immediate mechanism (like respiratory failure or cardiac arrest) would make all such deaths statistically identical, regardless of the actual disease. ICD-11 codes the underlying cause to make mortality data useful for disease prevention.

answers.text: Pneumonia, because it is the most recent acute diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pneumonia here is the intermediate cause (Part Ib), not the underlying cause. It developed because of the COPD, which initiated the entire chain of events leading to death.

answers.text: COPD, because it is the underlying cause that initiated the chain leading to death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The underlying cause — the lowest occupied row in Part I of the certificate — is what gets the ICD-11 code. COPD initiated the chain (COPD → pneumonia → respiratory failure), so it is coded.

answers.text: All three conditions should each receive a separate ICD-11 code

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While all three conditions appear on the certificate in Part I, only the underlying cause is coded for mortality statistics. The causal chain is documented, but a single code represents the fundamental cause of death.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: ICD-11 codes the underlying cause of death, found in the lowest occupied row of Part I. In the chain COPD → pneumonia → respiratory failure, COPD is the underlying cause.
Exactly. ICD-11 codes the underlying cause — the condition at the bottom of the Part I chain — because that is what makes mortality data meaningful for public health.

interactions.label: A woman is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident and

params.question: A woman is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident and dies despite resuscitation. The attending physician is certain the cause of death is haemorrhagic shock from a ruptured spleen. Can the physician issue the MCCD directly?

answers.text: Yes, because the cause of death is medically clear and documented

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Medical clarity of the cause does not override the legal requirement. Road traffic accidents are unnatural deaths, and all unnatural deaths — regardless of how obvious the mechanism — must go through the medicolegal process.

answers.text: Yes, provided the physician records the injury mechanism and accident details on the form

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Documenting the mechanism on the form does not change the legal category. Any accidental, homicidal, or suicidal death is unnatural and must be referred for inquest and possible forensic autopsy before certification.

answers.text: No, because road traffic accidents are medicolegal cases requiring forensic investigation before certification

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Road traffic accidents are unnatural deaths. Regardless of how clear the medical cause appears, the body must be referred to the police or a magistrate. Certification occurs only after the forensic process is completed.

answers.text: No, because the patient was never under the physician's care during a final illness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While technically true, this is not the primary reason. The real barrier is that this is an unnatural death (accident), which mandates medicolegal referral. Even if the physician had been treating the patient, an unnatural death still requires referral.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the key rule: any unnatural death — accidental, homicidal, or suicidal — must be referred for medicolegal investigation, regardless of how medically clear the cause of death is.
Right. The common thread for all referral cases: whenever the manner of death is unnatural or uncertain, your job is to report it, not to certify it.

interactions.label: Under the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, a living donor who is a near rela

params.question: Under the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, a living donor who is a near relative of the recipient requires approval from the Authorisation Committee before donating an organ.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Near-relative donors do not require Authorisation Committee approval — they need only consent and transplant team clearance. The Committee is involved only when the donor is a non-relative or in a swap arrangement, where its role is to confirm the donation is voluntary and not a disguised commercial transaction.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Near-relative donors (spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, or grandchild) need only give consent and receive transplant team approval. The Authorisation Committee is required only for non-relative donors and swap arrangements, to confirm there is no commercial motive.

metadata.title: Under the Transplantation of Human Organ

interactions.label: A financially distressed daily-wage labourer agrees to donate a kidney to an unr

params.question: A financially distressed daily-wage labourer agrees to donate a kidney to an unrelated wealthy recipient in exchange for money to settle his debts. He signs a consent form after being explained the procedure and risks. Which ethical principle is MOST directly compromised in this scenario?

answers.text: Beneficence, because the surgery does not benefit the donor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the surgery does not directly benefit the donor, beneficence primarily concerns the recipient's welfare. The core violation here is about the quality of the donor's consent, not the balance of medical benefit.

answers.text: Non-maleficence, because kidney removal exposes the donor to surgical harm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Surgical risk exists in all living donations, including altruistic ones with full autonomy. Non-maleficence is a consideration, but it is not what is specifically compromised by the financial pressure in this case.

answers.text: Autonomy, because financial desperation undermines truly voluntary consent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Although a consent form was signed, genuine autonomy requires a decision free from coercion. Financial desperation effectively compels the donor, making the consent a formality rather than a free choice. This is exactly why THOTA bans payment for organ donation.

answers.text: Justice, because the organ is not being allocated through the NOTTO waiting list

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Justice concerns are relevant here (wealthy recipients bypassing the system), but the most direct violation is to the donor's autonomy. The scenario specifically highlights financial pressure compromising voluntary consent.

overallFeedback.feedback: Focus on the donor's situation: he signed a consent form, but was his decision truly free? Financial desperation compromises autonomy, making consent a formality. That is why THOTA bans payment — to protect genuine voluntary consent.
Well analysed. Even when formal consent is obtained, financial pressure can render it meaningless — a key reason why THOTA criminalises organ trading rather than merely regulating it.
